A_target.statement: Every comparison-based [[Definition:Sorting Algorithm|sorting algorithm]] on $n$ elements makes $\map \Omega {n \log n}$ comparisons in the worst case.

B_source.statement:
Let $T$ be a [[Definition:Binary Tree|binary tree]] with $L$ [[Definition:Leaf of Tree|leaves]].
Then the [[Definition:Depth of Tree|depth]] of $T$ is at least $\log_2 L$.

substitutions.the binary tree: the decision tree of the algorithm, branching on each comparison outcome
substitutions.the leaves of the tree: the possible output permutations, of which there are n factorial

derived.the depth bound: at least log_2(n!) comparisons in the worst case
derived.the estimate of the logarithm: log_2(n!) is on the order of n log n, by Stirling

object_map.reformulation: Encode the algorithm's execution as a path in a binary tree, turning a running-time bound into a bound on tree depth.

validity_conditions: A comparison-based algorithm is faithfully modelled by a binary decision tree, since its control flow depends only on comparison outcomes.
Every permutation must be reachable as a distinct leaf, or two inputs requiring different outputs would be treated identically, so the tree has at least n factorial leaves.
The bound applies only to comparison-based algorithms; methods using the values directly, such as radix sort, are not modelled by such a tree and are not covered.
proof_plan: Model the algorithm as a binary [[Definition:Decision Tree|decision tree]], each internal node a comparison and each branch an outcome.

Each of the $n!$ input orderings requires a different output permutation, so reaches a distinct leaf.
Hence $L \ge n!$.
By the source result, the worst-case number of comparisons is at least $\log_2 \paren {n!}$.
